t: Minimum Number of Days to Eat N Oranges — Memoized Recursion over Divisor States
o: Each day you may eat 1 orange, or if the current count n is divisible by 2, eat n/2 oranges, or if divisible by 3, eat 2*(n/3) oranges. You want the minimum number of days to reach exactly 0. For example, with n = 10: eating 1 gives 9 (divisible by 3), then eating 6 leaves 3, eating 2 leaves 1, and one final day eats the last orange — 4 days total. With n = 6: eat 3 (halving), then from 3 eat 2, then 1 — 3 days. The constraint n up to 2*10^9 rules out any linear DP over all values; however, notice that repeatedly applying /2 and /3 from a single starting value reaches only about O(log^2 n) distinct numbers, so we can memoize just those.
k: Eating oranges one at a time until reaching a multiple of 2 or 3 is always optimal — you never need more than 2 consecutive single-orange days before a bulk move.
The state space is tiny: starting from n, all values reachable via repeated floor division by 2 and 3 number only O(log^2 n), so memoization on those states suffices even for n = 2*10^9.
From a non-divisible n, f(n) = min(n % 2 + 1 + f(n/2), n % 3 + 1 + f(n/3)) captures 'eat singles to reach divisibility, then take the bulk action'.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute-force BFS over all counts
a.i: Treat each orange count as a graph node with edges for the three allowed moves, and run BFS from n to find the shortest path to 0. This directly models the problem but visits up to n distinct states, which is infeasible for n near 2*10^9. It is included only to build intuition; it will TLE on large inputs.
s: Initialize a queue with n and dist[n] = 0.
Pop count c; if c == 0 return its distance.
Push c-1, and c/2 or 2*(c/3) when divisible, with distance + 1.
a.t: O(n) time and space — every count from 0 to n can be enqueued once, which is far too slow for n up to 2*10^9.
a.sp: O(n) for the visited map and queue.

a.n: Approach 2: Memoized recursion on divisor-reachable states (optimal)
a.i: Key observation: if n is not divisible by 2 or 3, the best plan is to eat single oranges only until you hit a multiple of 2 or of 3, then take that bulk action. So f(n) = min(n%2 + 1 + f(floor(n/2)), n%3 + 1 + f(floor(n/3))), with base cases f(0)=0, f(1)=1, f(2)=2. Every recursive call roughly divides n by 2 or 3, so the set of distinct arguments has size O(log^2 n) (~a few thousand for n = 2*10^9), making memoization extremely fast. One must be careful NOT to write f(n) = min(f(n-1)+1, ...) naively with plain recursion, since the f(n-1) chain would be linear-depth without memoization on intermediate values.
s: Define f(n): minimum days to eat n oranges.
Otherwise compute min(n%2 + 1 + f(n//2), n%3 + 1 + f(n//3)).
Memoize results in a hash map keyed by n.
a.t: O(log^2 n) time — each call branches into n/2 and n/3, so at most ~(log2 n)*(log3 n) distinct states are ever computed, each in O(1).
a.sp: O(log^2 n) for the memoization map plus recursion stack of depth O(log n).

w: In an interview, go straight to the memoized divisor recursion after noting that a linear DP cannot handle n up to 2*10^9; mention the BFS model briefly as intuition. Common pitfalls: writing f(n) = min(f(n-1)+1, ...) recursively without memoizing every intermediate value (stack overflow / TLE), forgetting base cases f(0)=0, f(1)=1, f(2)=2, and assuming greedy 'always divide when possible' works (it does not — e.g., n=10 requires eating down to 9 first). Edge cases: n=1 (answer 1), n=2 (answer 2), powers of 2 and 3. Follow-ups might ask to prove why at most 2 consecutive single-eat days suffice (any 3 consecutive single days can be replaced by one halving or thirding move without increasing cost), or to reconstruct an optimal schedule.
